speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The house is in committee.

I think I should make a few remarks with regard to the statements that were put on Hansard within the last few minutes by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The statement which has been largely read to the committee this evening was in substance put on the record on June 3 last and was also put on the record a year ago. At the time it was placed on the record a year ago I called attention to some remarks which had been made which were not entirely in accordance with the facts. I am going to say this evening that, while the record which was placed on Hansard-
On a point of privilege, to what statements is the minister referring?

I am coming to that and will indicate what they were. The hon. member has been reading to the committee letters that were received by the federation of agriculture from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and has referred to discussions which took place between myself and the president of the federation. The letters in themselves in so far as they were read are, of course, in accordance with the facts. But my hon. friend did not tell all the story, as he himself knows.

You
finish it then.

I will finish it and when I have finished the hon. member may have something else to say. The position which was taken by the hon. member and read on to the record previously was to this effect, with regard to the agreement entered into for the sale of the nitrogen products plants at Calgary and in the Niagara peninsula:
If hereafter for any reason the (U.K.) government at any time or times within twenty (20) years from the date hereof shall desire or determine to lease or dispose of said plant or any department or part thereof except to "any government within the British empire or North America," N.A.C.L. shall be given the first opportunity.
The impression has been left with the committee by the hon. member that governments
did not have any opportunity to buy this plant, and that the farm organizations had no opportunity to buy it. The fact is that the president of the federation of agriculture carried on a correspondence, first, with the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, and when he felt that the plant would probably be sold if something further were not done he came to the Minister of Agriculture and carried on conversations with him in regard, to the matter. As a result of the representations made, I met the farm organizations from western Canada, at the suggestion of the president of the federation, and discussed with them the whole question whether arrangements could be made for the disposal of this plant to some government or to some farm organization in western Canada. It is true that, strictly speaking, the farm organization probably could not, under the terms of the agreement, have obtained the plant directly. But there is a suggestion, that governments could have retained possession of the plant.
A letter has been read on to Hansard to the effect that the Alberta government did make inquiries, but I notice that the hon. member did not follow through, or give any indication to the committee or the country of what the final outcome of that correspondence was or whether the government of Alberta pressed its desire to obtain the plant which was located in Alberta. My memory of the discussions and my understanding of them is this, and I know something whereof I speak because I went to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply myself and asked him to hold these plants in possession of the government until such time as every possible concern in western Canada that might want to purchase the plants had an opportunity to do so. It was only after the president of the federation of agriculture came to me personally-and I am sure he will take no exception to my saying so tonight, and he will so state anywhere- and said it did not appear that any arrangement could be made to have these plants handled by any of the organizations in western Canada, or by the governments in western Canada, that the plant was disposed of. We had exhausted every possible attempt that could be made to see to it that if any government or farm organization desired to take over these plants an opportunity would be given them to do so.
I agree that, strictly speaking, there are terms in the agreement which may have made it difficult, if the company had desired to make it difficult for this kind of thing to happen; but there was no indication given to the government or to the minister, so far as I know, that the company itself would
Supply-Agriculture

have objected to the operation of this plant by farm organizations or by a government. The fact of the matter is that every farm organization in western Canada-and some of them have considerable funds of money running into millions of dollars-examined into the possibility of taking this plant over and operating it, and decided, without any exception whatsoever, that they had no desire to do so. The government itself examined into the possibilities of operating the plant-
The federal government?

Yes. The federal government also examined into the possibility. I do not say that the federal government arrived at the decision which it did on the basis of the possibility of operating it; the federal government took the position that we were not desirous of going into that type of business in the western part of Canada.
The suggestion has been made that when we were discussing this question before, I stated that the chief reason for it was the fact that the greater part of the product had to be exported. It was not the idea that the product had to be exported that had anything in particular to do with the matter; it was the fact that if we were to operate the plant as a government we would operate it in opposition to plants being operated in other areas in other countries, not to serve our own people, because the product which is an ingredient of fertilizer is not a product which is used, in quantities comparable witfi the possible production of the plant, in the fertilizer that would be useful in the western part of Canada. It is an ingredient of fertilizer which is used to a considerable extent in parts of eastern Canada and in parts of the United States. The product which is obtained in the United States for that purpose is partly provided locally and partly obtained from Chile. If we had undertaken the operation of that plant it would have meant that as a government we would be operating a plant which would not serve any real purpose in so far as the farmers of western Canada were concerned, and which would take us into competition within another country and with other organizations that were producing similar ingredients-

The
Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company are doing very well.

I do not know whether they are doing particularly well out of the plant or not; I am not in a position to say, but I am in a position to say this, that my 
hon. friend again threw out the suggestion that they might close it up. Well, if they are doing so well in it, why would they close it up? As a matter of fact, on the previous occasion when this matter was under discussion I said, in as definite terms as I could state it, that when I suggested out on the coast that there might be a possibility of the plant being closed up I immediately received a telegram from those who were operating the plant saying that it would not be closed up, that it would be operated. So far as I know, it will be operated. The plant is being operated there; but the point I wish to make is this. The government decided, as a matter of policy, that it would not operate that kind of plant. That is not the policy of the group in the opposition that are raising this question. Their policy is that they should purchase and operate plants of this kind in order to serve-
For the benefit of the people of that part of the country.

My friend says, "for the benefit of the people of that part of the country". He refers particularly to Saskatchewan. There was not a thing in the world to prevent the government of that province from buying this plant had they wished to do so. He says the service that is to be given is to be given to thousands upon thousands of farmers in Saskatchewan. If that plant could be of service to thousands and thousands of farmers in Saskatchewan, why did not the socialist government which believes in that kind of thing buy the plant at Calgary and operate it? It could have operated it just as successfully as this government could have done or as any other government could have done. I would suggest to them that when they are advocating governments taking over plants of this kind they take a look at what their own government is doing in connection with these matters in the province in which they live. If they do that, they will find that there is not very much that the government has taken over out there and tried to operate as a government, which has been of assistance to thousands and thousands.
That is not what the minister says when he goes to Saskatchewan.

They took over a little box factory which employs some fifty or sixty men and they took over a brick plant at Estevan, which is operated on clay from which you cannot make good brick, as everyone in the western part of Canada understands.

Supply-Agriculture
On a point of order, I am wondering just what the plants that are taken over in Saskatchewan have to do with fertilizer.

I know it has this to do with fertilizer. If the government of Saskatchewan had wanted to operate a plant and produce fertilizer it could have done so; it could have operated it. But of course they had no desire to do so for the same reason that others did not desire to do so.
If there happens to be some concern in Canada that,-by operating a plant in cooperation with some other plant, can make a success of operating it, then I do not know of any reason why they should not operate it.
There is a great deal of argument as to what they will charge farmers in western Canada for the product. There is far more necessity for considering just to what extent the plant could be used by farmers in western Canada even if it were operated. By whomever it was operated, that plant would produce very much more in the way of an ingredient of fertilizer than western Canada will use. If it is to operate at all it will operate for the production of fertilizer for somebody somewhere else, and therefore it was not so much a matter of concern to this government from the point of view of the western farmer as has been made out.
All I want to say is that those who believe in government ownership and control of all industries in Canada, when they have an opportunity to take over a plant that is considered so valuable to the farmers of western Canada as the plant at Calgary is considered by them to be, should have made a much better effort to take it over and operate it themselves and provide the farmers with this much needed fertilizer about which we have been hearing.

I wish to ask the minister two questions. I think it might be well-and it may be obvious-to say that I have no intention of entering into a debate with respect to fertilizer. Is it not true that when that plant was operating during the war and making ammonia, over ninety per cent of the product was exported and used largely on the gulf coast of the United States? In other words, ten per cent of it could be used in this country. Is it not true, that that plant, in one month's operation, could make all the ammonia which could possibly be used in fertilizer for the whole of Canada and that, therefore, during the other eleven months it would be operating simply for export business for the gulf coast of the United States? Is that not the simple situation with respect to that plant?
That is a fact, yes.

Is it feasible today to fertilize the wheat areas in Saskatchewan? Is it not true to say that fertilizer is used today for smaller patches and more intensive cultivation? Is that not the fact? Could a man at any price fertilize a half-section of land? I do not know whether he could or not. I am simply asking the question to obtain information.

There are certain places where it would pay the farmer to fertilize his land, but not necessarily with the type of fertilizer that would be made from the product which is produced in Calgary. On the other hand, in an area, where the land has been cropped for fifty years and which will still grow fifty bushels of wheat to the acre, farmers are not very likely to spend very much money on fertilizer. All over western Canada there are areas where, whenever they get sufficient rain, without any fertilizer whatever they grow anywhere from thirty to fifty bushels an acre, and some of those lands have been under crop continuously for from forty to fifty years. Of course the time may come when some of the ingredients of that soil will be used to such an extent as to make it absolutely necessary to fertilize it with something, but there has been no suggestion that any considerable amount of the product of the Calgary plant could be used for the purpose of improving cropping conditions in western Canada.

It has been proved beyond doubt that the experimental station in Saskatoon, at the university, which has used fertilizer for the last five or seven years, has increased thereby the crop yields from six to eight bushels an acre.
Is that from the ammonia plant?

Yes. It uses a considerable portion of fertilizer from this plant. The minister tried to indicate that this type of fertilizer is not used in western Canada. It is, and we have been short of fertilizer in the west ever since 1942. This year when I was at home at Easter the man who sells fertilizer in the area I represent came and told me that if I wanted fertilizer for 1948 I would have to put in my order immediately. He said that unless I had the order in within a short time I had very little chance of getting fertilizer in 1948. There is a shortage of fertilizer in western Canada. There was a shortage this year and there will be a shortage next year. The minister is just trying to wash the thing out, but I am afraid
Supply-Agriculture

he cannot do so as far as the farmers of western Canada and the farmers in eastern Canada -are concerned, because they realize more than ever the need of fertilizer. They realize that the fertility of the soil in the country has been going down. Yields have been going down in many areas simply because we have not learned how to use fertilizer to the extent to which it has been used in Europe and in other parts of the world. Anyone who has gone to Europe and has seen the use of fertilizer there, and the yields obtained from the intelligent application of fertilizer, must realize that we have to use fertilizer more and more in this country if we are to maintain the fertility of the soil.
We had in this house a committee set up in the early days of the war, and that committee recommended to the government that these fertilizer plants should be maintained. On that committee the majority of the members were government supporters. As soon as the war was over, however, as the minister stated, the government had no further interest in maintaining the government plants and sold them. That is the whole story. They were not interested in maintaining these government plants or in seeing that fertilizer was produced here so that it could be sold to the farmers at prices which would enable them to use it.

That is part of the story but not the whole story. No one else was interested in keeping them either. No one else was interested in buying them. Those who, it was thought, might be interested were consulted in the matter and, after examination, they said they were not interested.
Again the minister is not stating the whole truth because the plant at Welland-
I am speaking of the western plant.

-was sold before the people out there knew it was sold. They did not know it had been sold until they saw reports in the papers. The government had given an assurance to those people that, before the plant was sold, they would be notified. Not only that, but the minister himself stated in a letter that the government did not intend to sell the plant but intended to operate it. But they did not carry out their word.
I would ask my hon. friend to stick with the area he is interested in.

I am sticking with a matter that is of interest to the whole country. I am 
not interested in western Canada alone; I am interested in agriculture throughout the country.

There is not an organization in eastern Canada that has control of government that believes in government ownership and control of plants of that kind. There is only one place in Canada where that condition exists, namely in Saskatchewan, and the government of Saskatchewan, which believes in that policy, had no interest in buying this plant.
Quite right, but the plant was not built in Saskatchewan. If it had been they would have been interested in it. The plant was in Alberta.
They took some interest in the meat packing plant in Edmonton. Why should they not take an interest in the plant in Calgary?
Again the minister is not stating the truth. The plant in Edmonton is a cooperative.
My hon. friend is not stating the facts when he says that I am not speaking the truth.
I did not say the minister was not speaking the truth.
Better read Hansard.
I said the government did not carry out their promise.

The government of
Saskatchewan took an interest in the opening up of the plant in Edmonton and guaranteed the funds of the farmers cooperative that operates the plant. So did this government. But not only did the Saskatchewan government do that. Ever since, they have been taking credit for what has happened in those plants. As a matter of fact, this government put up much more than the provincial government of Saskatchewan put up, and negotiated all contracts for the sale, and if the government of Saskatchewan could take an interest in the plant in Edmonton, why could it not take an interest in the plant in Calgary?
I might ask the minister the same question. If his government could take an interest in the plant in Edmonton, why not take an interest in the plant in Calgary?
We did. We arranged for its building.

You sold it.

Supply-Agriculture

I am not going to have my province slighted. As I understand it, the socialist government, according to the statement of the hon. member who last spoke, did not take an interest in this plant for the reason that it was located in Alberta. That is one of the queerest reasons I have heard advanced for anything. The reason the plant is in Calgary is the fact that it uses natural gas. I say to my hon. friend, your government's money would have been just as good as anyone else's if it had been offered to this government as purchase price. I go a long way with you in some of your ideas, but let us not say that your socialist government in Saskatchewan is afraid, ashamed

what should the word be?-to deal with us in Alberta. We will use you well and give you a profit on every deal you make with us. You will be treated all right.
The hon. member has little to say about the government of Alberta.
I will make a speech on that if you want me to. I think they are a splendid government.
Much better than Saskatchewan.

This vote is for $826,255 for plant products-seeds, feeds, fertilizers, insecticides, fungicides control, including a grant of $31,000 to the Canadian Seed Growers' Association. There is an increase of $111,999 over last year. I presume that is for fertilizer subsidy. I notice that an order in council. P.C. 2084, was passed on May 19, 194/, which deals with subsidies in connection with fertilizer chemicals, and so on. How are these subsidies operated? What is the procedure?
This new order in council does not represent any change in policy?
No, there has been no *mange up to date. I would not guarantee that there will not be any change during the year, but there has been none up to date.

I think the Minister of Agriculture was unfair in his remarks to the hon. member for Assiniboia. I should like to remind the minister that on June 3, at page 3758 of Hansard, he declined to discuss the question, when he said:
I should like to suggest that an address like the one to which we have just listened is an appropriate one to have in connection with these estimates, but the place to have it is on the item of fertilizers.
I might remind the committee that we are now on item 20, and the minister has not been before the committee for very many hours. I think he will agree that usually he spends as many hours on the first item as he has now spent in getting nineteen items through, and the committee has cooperated by spending very little time on the general item. The hon. member for Assiniboia, I think quite correctly, was prepared to discuss this question of fertilizers, because it does affect the whole field of agriculture. I have read over the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia on June 3, and it is pretty clear to me that there has been very little if any repetition this evening. He has covered new material; and the fact that the minister has found it difficult to answer the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Assiniboia and also the hon. member for
415S
Supply-Agriculture

Melfort would indicate that this is a matter of national concern. The fact that the hon. member for Assiniboia discussed it a year ago is immaterial, for I think it is the duty of hon. members to discuss these matters year after year until they get some redress. Would the minister make some comment on the complaint of the hon. member for Melfort that it is impossible to have any assurance of supplies for 1948 in the western provinces?
There is no reason whatever to doubt that supplies will be available for the coming year.

I wonder if I might draw the minister's attention and have his interest in regard to the sending of an inspector by his department to California at least once a year. The seed potato growers in my district go to California, where there are seed plots planted. There some eighty acres of land have been set aside for the growing of seed potatoes. The various states take plots of land and plant their seed potatoes there. The states participating in the scheme send inspectors to examine and look aftef the plots; then at the proper time buyers from all over the country visit those plots and buy the potatoes they desire. Apparently we do not recognize what is being done in the United States. I am not familiar with what takes place in the mari-times, but I know that in British Columbia they go to considerable expense to send men to California, not only to plant the seed, but to look after the potatoes until they mature. This is being done with the view of building up a trade in seed potatoes, and I might say it is doing very well. But our growers feel that some notice should' be taken of it by the Department of Agriculture and that it should be recognized by the dominion government. So that I am asking the minister if he will take note of this and give the matter some consideration, to see if it would not be possible to have one of our own inspectors go to California and cooperate with the growers of seed potatoes in British Columbia.

In recent years we have had at least four persons go to California, including one of the gentlemen sitting in front of me tonight, checking their operations and bringing back whatever information can be obtained.
To speak of another product than potatoes, as hon. members from the west know we have even multiplied the sawfly-resistant type of wheat in California and brought back the product for utilization here. In other words, we have been keeping in touch; but I will take under consideration the suggestion that

has been made that we should do even more in that direction, and supply more information.
Are the government carrying on any experiments in connection with spraying from aeroplanes in regard to weed control?

The item with which we are now dealing is not 'the item under which that information can be obtained, and those who are specialists in those matters are not here at the moment. However, considerable experimental work has been done, as the hon. member knows, in connection with killing weeds by sprays; and it has been extremely successful. I am not in a position to say whether it has been done to any considerable degree with aeroplanes. I believe it has been done mainly by vehicles moving on the ground, but elsewhere it has been carried out by aeroplanes, and no doubt they could be utilized here if it were thought advisable to do so.

It was my intention to ask a number of questions concerning experiments in the use of chemicals for the destruction of weeds, but since the minister has indicated it is not possible to discuss that matter under this item, may I ask under which item it would be proper to ask those questions?
That would come under botany and plant pathology, item 8, which we covered last night.

I feel that this matter is of sufficient importance that, even though the item may have been dealt with, I should hope the minister might make provision later on for some discussion. I find a great deal of confusion today in newspapers and other publications. The farmers are inquiring about the success or otherwise of the use of certain chemicals, and the sum total of it is that they are rather bewildered.

To come back to the question of fertilizer, the hon. member for Calgary West asked the minister if it would be unreasonable to expect that western farmers in large sections of Saskatchewan and the prairie provinces could not use fertilizer, at any rate, because it would not be practical to do so. I have here a scientific report showing the effects of phosphatic fertilizers on summer fallow wheat crop in certain areas of Saskatchewan. In the controlled tests covering the years 1939 to 1943, using approximately fifteen pounds to the acre of 1148, the average cost per acre would be forty-six cents. The return averaged 6-8 bushels to the acre. If we figure that out on a dollar basis

Supply-Agriculture
it would make a return of S9.18 per acre to the farmer for his expenditure of forty-six cents.
I would say, too, with all due deference to the minister's ability as Minister of Agriculture. I saw him out on the ball diamond last night, where he did some skidding around. But. in my opinion he has done even a better job of that tonight.
I believe I have put on the record what the government did with respect to fertilizer. I say the statement of the minister in regard to Saskatchewan where we have a C.C.F. government. that they should have undertaken this proposition of buying up government owned plants, is not sufficient, and is beside the point. I might say to him that his own government has many crown corporations. I refer specifically to the Polymer Corporation, where they have reduced the price of synthetic rubber three times. One of the last reports I received from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply was that it is selling at around sixteen cents a pound. They have reduced the production costs of synthetic rubber by one-half since they went into operation. We could have done the same thing in regard to fertilizers.
Did not competition reduce that price?
No competition there.
Oh, yes; there is the competition of natural rubber. That is what reduced the price of synthetic rubber.
They are still making a profit at the new price.
I do not doubt that they are.
They do not produce it on farms, anyway.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There must not be so much conversation between members.

There is one other thing concerning which I take issue with the minister. He got a little out of his orbit when he referred to clay products in my constituency at Estevan. We are trying to do a good job in Saskatchewan, with our C.C.F. government there; we are trying to do a good job for our people. It is not fair for the Minister of Agriculture to state in the house that he is not a ceramics engineer, but that our clay in Saskatchewan utilized at our clay products plant at Estevan is not suitable for th# making of brick. My opinion is entirely different.
Well, I used to be minister in charge of it.
That is why they went on the rocks.
And I happened to know that the brick is not used extensively.
Maybe that is why the Liberal government decided to sell it out for one dollar to private interests.
The Liberal government [DOT] never owned it.

You
owned part of it. You put a lot of cost into it-several hundred thousand dollars.
No, you are dreaming.

My
information from ceramic engineers is that not only can we make brick, tile and face brick, but we can also make different types of pottery.

Would the minister make a statement with regard to negotiations with the Canadian seed growers' association? A few years ago, apparently in error, part of the requirements of the association were overlooked. While we had a supplementary vote later on, my recollection is that the association did not receive as much as they normally should have had for their operations. Would the minister indicate whether correspondence with the association indicates that they are satisfied with the grant, and also whether consideration cannot be given to increasing the grant, in view of the contribution to Canadian agriculture by the seed gowers association? I think the vote is altogether too small. Are they satisfied with the adjustment?

Two years ago there was a misunderstanding in the matter of supple-mentaries. Last year that was adjusted. Everything the seed growers asked for was provided for them. I am not saying they could not spend more money to good advantage. But everything they have asked for, to date has been provided for them; and they are not asking for more at the present time.
I gather from the minister's tone that if they have places where they could spend additional money a request from them in the near future would receive favourable consideration.
I did not say that.

It is not my intention to bring back the fertilizer issue. I should
Supply-Agriculture

like to say to hon. members to my left that if they canvassed southwestern Ontario they might be able to buy a considerable quantity of fertilizer probably at less than cost price, because it cannot be used this spring on account of flood conditions. Then again I would suggest that if they had enough copies of todajr's Hansard scattered around the west it might eventually become very good fertilizer.
I wish to ask the minister one question regarding the feeds situation in eastern Canada. I know he made a statement last night, but in view of the tremendous shortage which might be expected this year, which is estimated at nearly 70,000,000 bushels of oats and barley alone, and which means a critical situation, I would urge him to make a definite statement in the very near future, if he cannot do so tonight, in regard to the government's policy.

I think I said last night, before concluding my remarks with regard to feed, that for at least another three weeks it would be almost impossible for the government, or anyone, to be satisfied as to what conditions will be in relation to feed.
We know at this stage that there will not be within at least fifty per cent of the amount of feed which will be required in eastern Canada, as compared with last year. We must take account of the fact that of all feeds used last year about half was shipped in. We also know that the crop condition in western Cnaada, with regard to both acreage and seeding, and the present condition of the crop, is as good as it has been in some of our best years. But that can all change in the next three weeks. We are, of course, hopeful that it will not, and that it will go on and be a bumper crop.
If it is, then the government can announce a certain line of policy which would mean that we would move grain down east as rapidly as it can be moved. In any event, we will move whatever there is down as rapidly as arrangements can be made to have it moved. But in case there is any change in crop conditions out west, the policy would have to be different. At the present time I should not like to attempt to say what the policy will require to be, or will be.

I realize that the minister knows the seriousness of the situation. But I must point out that if a policy is not brought forward in sufficient time there is the possibility that a good deal of live stock in eastern Canada will be sold at reduced prices. If they know they have not the feed here they may not be willing to take chance on

waiting until the government policy is announced.

I am interested in obtaining some information with respect to class B fairs. I see where there are forty-three class B fairs across the dominion. How many are there in Ontario? How many are being added this year?

While we are looking up the information which has been asked for, I think I might place on Hansard a statement which I had intended to make. This is perhaps as good a time as any to give it.
Under the authority of orders in council P.C. 2294 and 2295 of June 6, 1947, the basis upon which assistance will be given to class A and class B exhibitions and .to winter fairs by the Department of Agriculture is now established. This basis has the support of the Canadian association of fairs and exhibitions, with which organization the question was discussed in detail some months ago. As in prewar years, financial support will be given by the department to all the above classes of fairs in featuring activities of junior farm club organizations and in securing judges. The main departmental grant to class A and class B exhibitions, with the same maximum limitations as applied in pre-war years will, however, in future be centred on financing capital expenditures rather than current expenditures as in the past. Owing to their limited opportunity to obtain revenue from gate receipts, et cetera, winter fairs may utilize the departmental grant for which they qualify in financing either capital or current expenditures.
Eligibility for classification as either class A or class B exhibitions in each province will, as in the past, be determined in consultation with the provincial department of agriculture. Among other things, the average prize money awarded by a fair in utility classes of live stock, poultry, grain, vegetables, fruit, dairy products and honey in the three years prior to that in which the application for such classification is made, and the location of the fair in relation to other fairs already classified, will be important factors fn determining eligibility.

Each exhibition association interested in securing assistance from the department toward its capital expenditures on improvements will be expected to submit its proposal in time to permit of agreement being reached prior to undertaking the work. Acceptance of an application will be conditional upon at least one-half of the cost of the undertaking being financed by the association itself.
It is evident that many exhibitions and fairs will wish to take advantage of this assistance in undertaking improvements, toward the cost of which the departmental grant available in one year would represent a very minor contribution. To enable them to finance such undertakings, the department is now authorized to enter into formal agreements covering departmental grants over periods in no case exceeding ten years. Each such agreement will be subject to final approval by the governor in council. I might explain that by saying that the amount for this purpose to a class B fair is SI,800 and to a class A, $2,500 a year. It will be possible by arrangement to have the entire amount over a ten-year period or less spent in the one year.
Do I understand that the $1,800 has to go to capital improvement?

The $1,800 has to go to the improvement of facilities that are being used by the fair board, and I presume that that could properly be called a capital expenditure. But if they wish to make, let us say, a $18,000 expenditure, or a $36,000 expenditure, $18,000 of which is to come from this government, then it can be arranged that ten yearly grants can be spent in the one year, but there would be no regular grants paid during that ten-year period. The same would be true with regard to the $2,500 grants provided for class A fairs.
Periodically, requests are received from exhibition associations for assistance in constructing buildings or other major capital undertakings, the cost of which would greatly exceed that which could be approved under the general plan of departmental assistance in two-way agreements. In such cases the department is now authorized, subject to the final approval of the governor in council in each case, to reach agreement with such associations, under which the departmental assistance over a maximum period of ten years will not exceed one-third of the total cost of the undertaking, and will be limited to a maximum annual amount of $10,000.
This means that over a ten-year period it might be possible for an arrangement to be made to spend $100,000, which would be provided by the federal government. In other words, if an expenditure of $300,000 was to be made and if an arrangement was made with the province to spend $100,000 and with the association or city concerned to take care of $100,000. the federal government might take care of $100,000 over that period of time, provided that, after discussions had taken place, the council could be convinced that this was the proper procedure to follow in that particular case.
In answer to the hon. member, I would say that there are thirteen class B fairs in Ontario. They are at Barrie, Belleville, Brampton, Galt, Kingston, Leamington, Lindsay, Port Arthur. Renfrew, Richmond, Simcoe, Stratford and Woodstock.
Is the department considering any class B fairs this year ?

There are some under consideration. The statement which I have just given outlines the conditions under which they may be admitted. It is based on their record for the past three years and on the discussions with the provincial governments.

I understand that an application has been made by Tees-water. Teeswater is strictly a rural district; you cannot by any stretch of the imagination find anything urban about that district. I have been led to believe that there is a probability that two class B fairs will be added this year, and these are what I would: class as semi-urban. My information may be wrong, but I understand that they are to be at Markham and Welland. I think I am justified in asking the minister to see that Teeswater does not miss out to those two places.
I understand that all three places have made application. Those applications are being considered but no decision has yet been reached.

The fair at Teeswater is not in my riding, being in Bruce, but I wish to say that it is considered to be one of the best, if not the best fall fair west of Toronto. It draws three times the crowd that other fairs do, and I think its reputation in the past ten years will substantiate that. I certainly ask the minister to give due consideration to this application. It is an absolutely rural fair, there being no cities within miles of it.

I wish to say something to the right hon. minister in regard to beef cattle. I realize that this has been discussed before and I intend to be brief. What I am urging is the opening of the cattle market to the United States. But, first, could the minister give me approximate figures for any year which he has as to the number of Argentine, United States and Canadian beef imported into Great Britain, and can he tell me the price spread which Britain is paying to these three countries? I know the highest price goes to the United States, the next to Canada, and the lowest price to the Argentine. At least that is my information.
I point to something else. In 1944 we
shipped to the United States dairy cattle to the value of over $4 million; in 1946 we shipped dairy cattle to the value of over $7 million. In other words, the increase was almost 100 per cent, and yet not one beef
animal was shipped during that period. What I am anxious to know is why the man who grows the beef is discriminated against in that particular way.
I intend to read two extracts from a copy of a letter which has come to my possession, a letter written by Mr. W. L. Clayton, undersecretary of state for economic affairs of the United States government. It is dated January 29, 1947, and was written to a United States senator. I may say that this letter was prompted by an inquiry made by a large rancher in southern Alberta to a senator whom he knew in Salt Lake City. He communicated with Mr. Clayton and this is the reply. He says:
The action taken by the Canadian government in 1942 prohibiting exports of cattle was designed to make available for export to England maximum quantities of beef and other meats.
It was in order to ensure the delivery of the large quantities of meat required during that critical period that the Canadian government undertook to buy and ship the meat on a gov- . ernment to government basis.
Then, skipping a portion of it which I do not consider relevant, I continue:
This procedure appears to have been continued as the most practicable and efficient means of meeting commitments later incurred in the Anglo-Canadian meat contracts. These contracts and similar ones which the United Kingdom has concluded with some of the other dominions are understood to have been motivated by 'the desire on the part of the United Kingdom to secure during 'the period of uncertainty both as to supply and price adequate supplies of foodstuffs at reasonable prices.
I do not think there is anything controversial so far. I continue:
In fact this government has pointed out to both the United Kingdom and Canada that it considers such long-term bulk purchasing contracts on a fixed price basis to be incompatible with plans for the removal of barriers to trade to which both governments have given their support.
It seems to me that that is almost selfevident as well. Then he goes on in the last paragraph as follows:
With regard to the department's attitude toward the importation of Canadian cattle, it is our desire that all war-time controls be ended as soon as the purposes for which they were imposed cease to exist. This is in accord with our commercial-policy objective of an expanding international trade open to private enterprise on a competitive and non-discriminatory basis. The Canadian government has expressed a similar attitude. Therefore, if the Canadian government should be willing to allow the exportation of cattle to the United States, the department would have no objection. Cattle imported into the United States would, of course, be subject to import duties as modified under the trade agreement act.
I mentioned that in 1944 we shipped $4 million worth of dairjr cattle and in 1946, $7
Supply-Agriculture

million worth. I was not referring to the purebred animals which are admitted into the United States duty free; I was referring to grade dairy cattle which went in under a duty of a cent and a half a pound or whatever it is. As the minister knows, the Mexican quota has been stopped because of foot and mouth disease in that country. The importation of cattle from there is closed at the present time. The suggestion I am making in all seriousness to the minister-I know he is sympathetically inclined to the idea-is that we should now, without further delay, get some shipments into the United States while the duty remains as it is. I realize fully that we shall be met with the difficulty with respect to supplying our contracts to the old country but this is what I greatly fear, with the greatest respect for the minister. I am not saying that the minister is devising a policy to hurt this country; I do not make stupid criticisms of that kind. I am quite sure that he feels he is doing what is in the best interest of the producers of this live stock; but I have seen a number of them lately. I am not referring to the small ones; I am referring to the large ones, and they have a real fear that if we cannot continue some flow of cattle across that line, we shall lose that market. In fact they state definitely that if this one-way traffic with Great Britain is continued until 1950 we shall lose that opportunity. As the minister agreed once before, the United States is our natural and logical market. The live stock producers greatly fear that something may happen in the meantime by which the opportunity of shipping to the United States may be lost. It is certainly simple. Once matters have adjusted themselves, where is Great Britain to look for her cattle? She will look in the cheapest place she can buy them. There is no doubt about that. We know we cannot raise beef cattle in this country at a price comparable with the Argentine, because in that country they do not have to do any feeding; they have year-round pasture. The only feeding that they do is a little finishing at the end of the road.
Having regard to the fact that Mexico is cut off not by their action, but by an embargo because of foot and mouth disease, I suggest, with the greatest respect, and with some hope,' that the minister find ways and means to permit some of our cattle to go across the line.
It is a well known fact that today there are more beef cattle on the hoof in Canada than there have ever been. I assume that much of the beef which goes to England is killed and shipped as chilled or perhaps frozen meat or something of that kind. Here is the place to 
put a lot of cattle which are on the hoof in western Canada today. I ask that the minister give this matter further consideration and that something may come of it even at this late day.

I should like to refer
to one or two of the remarks made by the hon. member. In the first place, the statement that was given by Mr. Clayton in the letter which was read is not news so far as we are concerned.	The attention of the
British government and also of the Canadian government was called to the possibility of a long-term contract being contrary to the spirit and letter of the international agreement or the international trade conference idea which had been presented to the united nations by the United States. But when they made that protest it was not made to the Canadian government; it was made to the British government, and the Canadian government was acquainted with the fact that they had made it. The British government was just as definite in its reply that it did not contravene the proposals which had been made by the United States; and I understand that, since the meeting was convened in Geneva to discuss the international trade organization arrangements, Mr. Clayton himself admitted that it was not contrary to the proposals which were made by the United States government for the convening of the international organization meeting, that this type of agreement be made. That is with regard to the one matter which is referred to and which I have seen in print in this form for the first time when this letter is handed to me, and I think it is only fair I should say that at the time the British government replied definitely to the statement and said that it was not in accordance with their understanding of the proposal. I understand now that the United States government and the British are in agreement that it is not, and that type of contract is in agreement with the principle laid down by the Americans in their proposal.
With regard to the matter of the Mexican boundary line being closed, that of course is a matter of fact. The Americans have refused to take cattle from Mexico because of a foot and mouth disease which they believe to be prevalent there and which they do not wish to have introduced into the United States.
The statement made with regard to prices obtained in Britain by the United States, the Argentine and ourselves is also correct.
I am not in a position to give the exact

amounts, but I think it is right to say they are paying the Americans more and the Argentine less.
What is the price so far as we are concerned?
About twenty-five.

I think the
figures are: United States, thirty-five; ourselves, twenty-five, and the Argentine, as low as eleven or thirteen.

It depends on quality;
twenty-five is the basic figure.
For us?

Yes, and again it must be remembered that ours is a long-time contract and the others are not. That is, one cannot tell at this stage how it will average over the entire period, but there is no doubt and never has been any doubt that cattle can be produced cheaper in the Argentine than in Canada and can be laid on the British market at a lower rate than we can produce them. There is no doubt that our natural market for a long period is in the United States.
The other factors being considered are related to the necessity for having beef supplied to Britain at present, and also have something to do with what we hope will be trading relations in the future as well as the fact that price control would be affected. But particularly, for the time being, the most important factor is the fact that this meeting is being held in Geneva, and we have stated in our discussions with everyone that, so far as this kind of contract and the arrangements for it are concerned, we think we should carry on as we are doing, at least until the conference is fairly well completed and we know the direction in which we are going as a result of the conference. That is the chief factor at the moment, although the main reason at the beginning was the reason stated in this letter; and the chief reason, I would say, still for continuing even to the end of the conference, is that Britain is in greater need of beef today than she has been for a considerable period of time. No later than today the representative of Britain was in my office inquiring with regard to the possibility of getting beef. Very little beef is going to Britain at the present time, as a matter of fact none, and little has gone over for some time. Apparently we are eating all the beef in Canada ourselves at present.

Could the minister give an approximate idea of the amount going to Britain over the last year
from the three countries? I do not want it in dollars; I would be content with rough percentages.

I meant from the United States to Britain and from the Argentine to Britain.

I have not those figures and I doubt very much whether you could get them. During the war the British were very particular in that regard: and I doubt very much whether we could get the figures. We do not know over here?
